neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and to the clinic location. States the correct month and year but is off by two days on the date and cannot identify the day of the week. MMSE 21/30: loses 2 points on orientation to time, 1 point on orientation to place (floor/building name), 3 points on delayed recall (0/3 words at 5 minutes with no benefit from category cues), 1 point on serial sevens, 1 point on sentence writing (produces a short, semantically impoverished sentence). Clock drawing test: numbers placed unevenly, clockwise sequence lost between 8 and 11; hands placed at 10:10 instead of the instructed time. Speech is fluent with several pauses to find words during the history. No paraphasias. Comprehension intact for two-step commands; difficulty with three-step commands. Recalls his professional career in detail but cannot recall recent family events (e.g., a grandchild's birthday party attended three weeks prior). Wife confirms he has repeated the same story about a project from his engineering career at least four times during the current visit.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact. Facial strength symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally without aids. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact in all extremities. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes, consistent with age and diabetes.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign. No frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No shuffling, festination, or magnetic gait pattern.
neurological_exam.additional: Wife reports a gradual change in her husband's memory over the past 18 months, becoming clearly noticeable approximately one year ago. He began forgetting recent conversations almost immediately, often repeating questions he had just asked. He forgot to submit a routine government form for renewing the family vehicle registration, something he had handled punctually for decades, resulting in a fine. Three months ago he left a tap running overnight, flooding the bathroom, and appeared unaware of having done so. He has become less engaged in discussions about engineering or current affairs, topics he previously dominated at family gatherings. Wife notes he is sometimes tearful when alone, which she believes is from frustration with his own memory. He has not got lost on familiar routes but is no longer driving for longer journeys. He sleeps well without acting out dreams. No visual hallucinations, no personality disinhibition, no falls.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory difficulties over the past 18 months, worsening over the last year, with increasing inability to manage household affairs
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Rajiv Mehta is a 68-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by his wife, Priya, for evaluation of progressive memory impairment. His wife first became concerned approximately 18 months ago when he began repeating questions and stories within short intervals, often unaware that he had just asked the same question minutes before. Initially she attributed this to stress after retirement, but the symptoms have worsened steadily despite the passage of time. Over the past year, the changes have been clearly functional: he forgot to renew the family vehicle registration — a task he had never missed in over 30 years — leading to a government fine. He twice failed to remember to take his diabetes medications despite them being placed in a clearly labelled weekly pill organiser, prompting the family to take over medication management. Three months ago he left a bathroom tap running overnight, causing significant flooding, and had no recollection of having used the tap. He has stopped managing household finances, a role he had held exclusively for 35 years; his son discovered multiple unopened bills when reviewing the family accounts. He no longer engages with engineering journals, a lifelong interest, and his wife notes he cannot follow multi-episode television series he was previously watching. He becomes frustrated and occasionally tearful when he is unable to recall something and is aware that his memory is failing him. He has not become lost on familiar routes and is able to dress and wash independently, though his wife supervises. His sleep is undisturbed; his wife reports no movements or vocalisation during sleep. There are no visual hallucinations, no personality disinhibition, and no aggressive behaviour. He has not had any episodes of fluctuating consciousness. He has had no falls, seizures, tremor, or gait disturbance. He was noted to have vitamin B12 deficiency four years ago and was started on supplementation, but he self-discontinued the supplements approximately 18 months ago, around the time his memory symptoms first became noticeable. He and his family are attributing his memory difficulties to the B12 issue and are hopeful that restarting supplementation will reverse his decline.

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic verbal memory is severely impaired: CVLT-II long-delay free recall at the 2nd percentile and immediate recall at the 4th percentile, reflecting a storage-type encoding deficit with limited benefit from recognition cues (9th percentile). Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 11th percentile) and semantic fluency (Category Fluency — Animals, 8th percentile) are below expected norms. Visuoconstructive ability and executive function (Trail Making A and B, 18th–28th percentile; Rey Complex Figure Copy, 27th percentile) are within low-normal range. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 17/30. Mood screening is borderline (GDS-15 5/15); the degree and pattern of memory impairment is disproportionate to any mood contribution

results.title: NIA-AA Research Framework: Toward a biological definition of Alzheimer's disease
results.authors: Jack CR Jr, Bennett DA, Blennow K, et al.
results.summary: The 2018 NIA-AA framework defines Alzheimer's disease biologically by the ATN profile: A (amyloid biomarkers — CSF Aβ42, amyloid PET), T (tau biomarkers — CSF phospho-tau, tau PET), and N (neurodegeneration — hippocampal atrophy, FDG-PET, total tau). A+T+ profile regardless of clinical stage constitutes Alzheimer's disease by biological definition.

results.title: Practice guideline update summary: Mild cognitive impairment (2018)
results.authors: Petersen RC, Lopez O, Armstrong MJ, et al.
results.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not recommended for amnestic MCI but are indicated for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer dementia. Cognitive training and vascular risk-factor management are recommended across the spectrum. Repeat neuropsychological testing at 6-12 month intervals supports monitoring.

results.title: Lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease (CLARITY AD trial)
results.authors: van Dyck CH, Swanson CJ, Aisen P, et al.
results.summary: Anti-amyloid antibody lecanemab reduced clinical decline by 27% over 18 months in participants with early AD (MCI or mild dementia) confirmed by amyloid biomarkers. ARIA occurred in 21.3% of treated patients. Key eligibility: amyloid-positive biomarkers, MCI or mild dementia stage, no significant MRI ARIA risk factors.

output.summary: The NIA-AA 2018 biological framework classifies Alzheimer's disease by ATN biomarker status independent of clinical stage. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated symptomatic benefit in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer dementia in randomized controlled trials. Disease-modifying anti-amyloid therapies (lecanemab, donanemab) reduce clinical decline in biomarker-confirmed early-stage disease; eligibility requires confirmed amyloid pathology and MRI screening for ARIA risk factors including APOE genotype and pre-existing microhaemorrhages.

interactions: Donepezil + Metformin: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Both may cause GI effects — monitor for additive nausea.
Donepezil + Ramipril: No clinically significant interaction. Both may contribute to orthostatic hypotension; advise care with positional changes.

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment with amnestic predominance; non-focal neurological examination

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics excluded; B12 low-normal at 214 pg/mL (within range, not causally sufficient); HbA1c 7.3% reflecting suboptimal diabetic control

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2-3) with temporoparietal-predominant cortical volume loss and mild white matter changes

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 and Aβ42/40 ratio with elevated p-tau 181 and total tau — A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive amyloid PET with moderate-to-frequent cortical amyloid plaque density, confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Impairment documented on a validated instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile and informant-confirmed decline from a previous level, staged by whether independence in instrumental activities is preserved (mild cognitive impairment) or lost (dementia)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in Alzheimer's disease and is not part of the standard dementia workup; no seizure or encephalopathy features to justify it
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication or cardiac symptoms in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT is inferior to MRI for dementia assessment and should not replace MRI when MRI is available and not contraindicated

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or raised intracranial pressure, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from a knowledgeable informant (spouse or family member who lives with the patient)
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs including CBC, CMP, TSH, and vitamin B12
Obtain structural brain MRI with volumetric/dementia protocol to characterise atrophy pattern and exclude NPH, vascular, and mass lesions
Perform comprehensive neuropsychological testing to objectively characterise and quantify the cognitive deficit
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF ATN profile or amyloid PET) to establish biological diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease
Assess safety: driving, medication self-management, financial management, and need for escalated caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family and initiate advance care planning and safety planning
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute the cognitive decline solely to vitamin B12 deficiency on the basis of a low-normal B12 level without completing the full dementia workup
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risks in this age group
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioural indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia patients
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage — memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease
key_reasoning_points: The clinical syndrome is a gradually progressive amnestic multi-domain dementia with IADL impairment, temporoparietal atrophy on MRI, and A+T+ CSF biomarkers — meeting NIA-AA 2011 criteria for probable Alzheimer's dementia and NIA-AA 2018 criteria for biological Alzheimer's disease

The low-normal vitamin B12 (214 pg/mL) is a deliberate red herring: it is within the reference range, the CBC shows no macrocytosis, and B12 deficiency does not produce the asymmetric hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA 3/2) or the A+T+ biomarker profile observed here

Metformin use is associated with impaired B12 absorption; checking methylmalonic acid or homocysteine would be prudent to exclude functional deficiency, but correcting B12 alone would not reverse an established neurodegenerative process with positive amyloid biomarkers

The patient and family's attribution of symptoms to B12 deficiency is a common cognitive distraction — the clinician must integrate the full ATN biomarker picture rather than anchor on a single reversible variable
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not required to make the clinical or biological diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease

Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer dementia; optimising glycaemic control and resuming B12 supplementation are warranted as modifiable comorbidity management but will not arrest neurodegeneration

red_herrings.data_point: Vitamin B12 214 pg/mL — low-normal, in a patient with prior B12 deficiency who self-discontinued supplementation 18 months ago, coinciding with symptom onset
red_herrings.intended_effect: The patient and family attribute all memory symptoms to B12 deficiency; a naive agent might defer the full AD workup, pending B12 supplementation trial
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: B12 is within the laboratory reference range (214 vs. 200-900 pg/mL); CBC shows no macrocytosis; the storage-type amnestic profile, asymmetric hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA 3/2), and A+T+ biomarker pattern are not consistent with isolated B12 deficiency. Functional B12 status should be confirmed with methylmalonic acid, and supplementation should be resumed, but B12 correction does not alter the AD diagnosis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward amnestic early AD dementia with characteristic hippocampal atrophy, A+T+ CSF biomarkers, and positive amyloid PET. One realistic red herring (low-normal B12 with history of prior deficiency and metformin use) plausibly diverts attention but does not obscure the diagnosis once the full workup is integrated.
